title: Improving the Stability of the Hierarchical Equations of Motion for Open Quantum Systems with Strong Coupling to Structured Bosonic Baths
authors: Salvatore Gatto, Samuel L. Rudge, Bokang Hou, Eran Rabani, Michael Thoss
abstract: The hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) approach is one of the most powerful methods avail- able to simulate the dynamics of open quantum systems. Although the HEOM approach has been shown to be stable and efficient in many parameter regimes and physical scenarios, it is also well known that the unavoidable finite truncation of the hierarchy can lead to fundamental numeri- cal instabilities for bosonic environments. In this work, we apply recently developed techniques to analyze these issues. We use an auxiliary Fock-space picture of the hierarchy to first identify the unbalanced hierarchy-raising terms responsible for the strong transient amplification associated with the non-normal algebraic structure of the HEOM generator. We then apply a non-unitary similarity transformation that converts these terms into balanced combinations of hierarchy-raising and hierarchy-lowering terms, thereby suppressing their numerical impact. We first demonstrate the efficacy of this approach via a spin-boson model with a simple Brownian oscillator spectral den- sity and subsequently extend the analysis to a structured spectral density, showing for both cases that the transformed HEOM approach allows simulations of much larger system-bath coupling than would otherwise be possible.
summary: This paper improves the numerical stability of the Hierarchical Equations of Motion (HEOM) method for open quantum systems. The authors identify that finite truncation leads to instabilities, especially with structured baths. They propose and demonstrate a non-unitary similarity transformation that mathematically balances the problematic terms, enabling simulations of much stronger system-bath couplings.
main_problem: The paper addresses fundamental numerical instabilities encountered when using the Hierarchical Equations of Motion (HEOM) approach to simulate open quantum systems coupled to structured bosonic baths.
main_result: The authors introduce a non-unitary similarity transformation that balances problematic hierarchy-raising terms, allowing for stable simulations with much larger system-bath coupling strengths than previously possible.
method: The core method involves analyzing the HEOM generator in an auxiliary Fock-space picture and applying a specific non-unitary similarity transformation to stabilize the evolution equations.
model_or_system: The study uses the spin-boson model ($	ext{HS} = \varepsilon\sigma_z + \Delta\sigma_x$) coupled to a bosonic bath ($	ext{HB}$), characterized by a spectral density $J(\omega)$. The analysis is general for open systems with Gaussian environmental coupling.
key_observables: The stability of the HEOM evolution, the two-time bath-correlation function $C(t)$, and the ability to simulate large system-bath coupling strengths.
important_parameters: System-bath coupling strength ($\lambda$), bath spectral density $J(\omega)$ (e.g., Brownian oscillator or structured density), and the truncation depth of the HEOM hierarchy.
main_assumptions: The theory assumes the environmental influence is Gaussian and the system-bath coupling is linear in the bath operators; the method itself is an extension to overcome numerical limitations of the HEOM truncation.
figures_summary: Not specified (The notes detail mathematical derivations and conceptual improvements rather than describing specific figure contents).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the model (spin-boson system), reviewing the HEOM framework, and finally detailing the application of the non-unitary similarity transformation to demonstrate the stabilization of the equations.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles a major computational bottleneck in simulating open quantum dynamics, providing a robust mathematical tool for studying strongly coupled quantum systems relevant to quantum optics and condensed matter physics.
